entry.title: How to get Quantitative Research roles in Taiwan or remote?

link.title: How to get Quantitative Research roles in Taiwan or remote?

entry.content:
Intro

In today’s blog post, I will share how to find quantitative research opportunities in Taiwan or remotely. More specifically, I will focus on hedge funds such as Maven Security, Optiver, WorldQuant, and Point72; trading firms such as Kronos, A&R Research Capital, VICI Holdings, UC Capital, and Holdwin Capital; and cryptocurrency exchanges such as Binance, Crypto.com, and Bitget.

Since these roles are highly competitive, I recommend applying only if you meet the following prerequisites:

  1. Participation in an IOI, IMO, or IPhO selection and training camp.
  2. An ICPC regional silver medal or above; for top hedge funds, a gold medal is preferred.
  3. A first-author paper at a top conference, such as ICML, ICLR, or NeurIPS.
  4. A top-5 ranking in WolrdQuant IQC Taiwan.
  5. Practical trading experience with a Sharpe ratio above 1.5.
  6. Buy-side quantitative research internship or full-time experience, rather than sell-side experience.

Moreover, most of them are either computer science or finance students at NYCU or NTHU who have received an Academic Excellence Award, or students majoring in computer science, electrical engineering, mathematics, physics, or finance at NTU.

Once you meet the above requirements, we can dive into how to prepare for interviews and eventually secure offers. First, I will outline the main sections below:

  1. Which NYCU courses are essential for entering this field?
  2. How can you write a curriculum vitae that helps you pass the first stage?
  3. How should you prepare for technical interviews?
  4. How should you prepare for behavioral interviews?
  5. What useful tips should you keep in mind throughout the application process?

Essential courses at NYCU

We can divide the main skills required for QR roles into four areas: mathematics, coding, statistics, and finance, with finance being optional. I recommend taking the following courses at NYCU.

For mathematics courses, I suggest taking:

  1. Linear Algebra (I), taught by Ming-Cheng Shiue
  2. Probability, taught by Ping-Chun Hsieh
  3. Discrete Mathematics
  4. Introduction to Analysis (I)
  5. Introduction to Analysis (II)
  6. Differential Equations
  7. Partial Differential Equations
  8. Stochastic Processes
  9. Optimization Algorithms, taught by Ping-Chun Hsieh

For coding courses, I suggest taking:

  1. Introduction to Algorithms, taught by Kai-Chiang Wu
  2. Competitive Programming(I)
  3. Competitive Programming (II)
  4. Competitive Programming(III)
  5. Machine Learning
  6. Deep Learning
  7. Deep Learning Labs
  8. Reinforcement Learning, taught by Ping-Chun Hsieh

For statistics courses, I suggest taking:

  1. Statistics
  2. Advanced Statistics

For finance courses, I suggest taking the graduate-level versions rather than similar undergraduate courses:

  1. Futures and Options
  2. Investment

Also, an important mindset is that instead of simply focusing on the knowledge taught in class, you should think more about the intuition behind it. For example, why is the sample variance intuitively larger than the population variance?

Write a Resume

I have five tips, as shown below:

  1. Fit the job description: Only include relevant and important experiences on your resume.
  2. Use a template: A good template allows you to focus on the content of your resume without worrying too much about its appearance.
  3. Use quantitative and well-known metrics: These metrics allow companies to objectively understand your impact, such as PnL, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, ICPC medals, paper publications, etc.
  4. Use strong verbs: Strong verbs help HR quickly understand your contribution and impact.
  5. Use LLMs to polish your writing: This can help reduce grammar errors.

Using the five strategies above can not only help you present your overall strengths but also help HR quickly determine whether you are suitable for the role.

Prep for Technical Interviews

To be more specific, technical interviews can be divided into two parts: the math part and the coding part.

For the math part, I strongly recommend the book Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews, written by Xinfeng Zhou, especially Chapters 2 to 4. You can look for this book through libraries or other legitimate sources.

For the coding part, I strongly recommend practicing on Codeforces and AtCoder, since problems on these platforms emphasize a comprehensive understanding of data structures and algorithms rather than simply applying templates.

For more company-specific questions, you can search on online platforms such as Reddit and 1Point3Acres. This can be really helpful when you have no idea how to start your preparation.

Prep for Behavioral Interviews

While some people may argue that these kinds of interviews are not very important, I still suggest preparing for them. This is because behavioral interview preparation can help you better understand what you truly want and what kind of work environment would make you feel satisfied.

I have two tips:

  1. STAR method: A framework that helps you tell clear and engaging stories.
  2. Collect Behavioral Questions: Collect and practice common behavioral questions in advance.

After preparing, you will have a deeper understanding of your future career and its working style, which is vital for building a long-term career path.

Useful Tips

In the following section, I recommend three methods for finding jobs:

  1. Mass-applying
  2. Build your LinkedIn profile
  3. Follow up

I will explain why I recommend these methods and what outcomes you can expect from using them.

Mass-applying

From an expected value perspective, if you want to receive more offers, you need to increase either:

  1. the number of jobs you apply for, or
  2. the probability of receiving an offer from each application.

By mass applying, you naturally increase the number of applications you submit. At the same time, you can also learn practical and general skills through the application and interview process, such as using the STAR method to answer behavioral questions. As a result, you may gradually improve your chances of receiving offers.

Therefore, I recommend this strategy as long as you can still maintain the same quality of preparation for each potential interview. In other words, mass applying is effective only if your probability of passing an interview does not decrease too much.

Build LinkedIn

The benefits are as follows:

  1. More job opportunities: One major benefit is that you may receive job opportunities from HR representatives or headhunters at other companies. This means your resume has a higher chance of being seen. Moreover, many overseas job opportunities are posted on LinkedIn rather than on platforms such as 1111, 104, or Yourator.
  2. A clearer understanding of job details: When you are unsure whether a job is suitable for you, you can send messages to people who are already working in that field. They are usually willing to share their experiences and answer your questions.
  3. A way to explore your dreams: When you feel confused about whether your career or life path is realistic, you can check whether someone else has taken a similar path before. If no one has, it may mean that you are a pioneer. Such a path may be full of thorns, but it may also lead to something meaningful.

Follow Up

Following up shows that you are proactive, which is a valuable quality during the application process. Therefore, I recommend following up on your application progress about one to two weeks after an interview. It can also help you estimate your timeline more clearly and feel less nervous.

For example, you may feel confused in the following situations:

  1. Before an interview: What will the interview be about? Will it focus on technical problems, such as LeetCode-style questions or probability, or behavioral questions, such as why you want to apply to this company?
  2. After an interview: Will I have another interview? After learning from the interview experience, can I do further research or work on a project to show my growth mindset? Can I also discuss what I learned with others?

Conclusion

In general, pursuing quantitative research roles is a very challenging path. Before even receiving online assessments, we often need to graduate from prestigious schools and have competitive awards or achievements. It is not enough to be someone who only crams knowledge overnight.

After passing the resume screening stage and receiving an invitation to the next interview, you still have to compete with many excellent candidates, some of whom may even have publications in top conferences.

However, I strongly believe in the following quote:

It is not our abilities that show what we truly are… it is our choices. –”Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets”

Many of us are willing to tolerate volatility in order to pursue higher returns, just like seeking excess returns in the market. Many of us also want to pay fewer taxes to a government we consider inefficient. For example, in Taiwan, overseas income is taxed only when it exceeds NTD 7,500,000.

Many of us are not satisfied with a stable but unhealthy work style in Hsinchu Science Park companies. Therefore, choosing a quantitative trading-related job is not only a career pursuit but also a way to express our beliefs.

link.title: Quantitative Finance Researcher Online Assignment (2026 VICI Summer Internship)

entry.content:
Intro

This post provides a step-by-step solution to the online assignment provided by VICI Holdings.

Data Observations

In the zero stage, we observe that the data distribution is very unbalanced and concentrated on class 0, both in the training and evaluation datasets. The detailed information is as follows:

  Train Data Eval Data
Class 0 54.24% 54.06%
Class 1 21.88% 21.19%
Class 2 23.88% 24.75%

As we can see, more than half of the data is concentrated in class 0. Therefore, we use the F1-score instead of accuracy for our evaluations because this metric is more appropriate for estimation in an unbalanced dataset.

Conclusion

TL;DR: By using ensemble models, applying LogisticSigmoid feature scaling, and using random search for hyperparameter tuning, we improved accuracy by about +9.86% (≈ +19.6% relative) and macro F1 by about +16.38% (≈ +41.3% relative) on the evaluation dataset.

F1-score Optimization

In the first stage, we build a basic linear model, SGDClassifier, using the scikit-learn library, without any regularization terms, special data transformations, or complex models, to serve as our baseline. We then compare the 11 linear and tree-based models listed on the sklearn.linear_model, sklearn.naive_bayes, sklearn.tree, and sklearn.ensemble pages, and select the models with the top three F1-scores on the evaluation dataset as our candidate models.

Model Structures

model train_accuracy train_macro_f1 eval_accuracy eval_macro_f1
HistGradientBoosting 0.62859 0.598935 0.59866 0.560088
RandomForest 1.0 1.0 0.58702 0.54218
ExtraTrees 1.0 1.0 0.585008 0.538936
RidgeClassifier 0.5799 0.507133 0.577786 0.520994
DecisionTree 1.0 1.0 0.526877 0.511301
PassiveAggressive 0.51688 0.496916 0.52054 0.505316
GaussianNB 0.509092 0.494076 0.516318 0.50131
Perceptron 0.411236 0.391859 0.429896 0.409868
SGD_LinearSVM 0.488353 0.397915 0.498656 0.396802
SGD_Logistic 0.491731 0.39739 0.501752 0.39657
LogisticRegression 0.53719 0.25302 0.537412 0.249521

From the experiment, we found that HistGradientBoosting, RandomForest, and ExtraTrees achieved higher F1-score values than the other seven models. Therefore, we selected them as our candidate models. In other words, ensemble methods are more powerful than linear models, naive Bayes models, and single-tree models in this problem.

Feature Scaling-1 (sklearn)

Next, we apply StandardScaler, QuantileTransformer, Normalizer, and KBinsDiscretizer from sklearn.preprocessing to generate different feature representations. The results are shown below.

preprocessor model train_accuracy train_macro_f1 eval_accuracy eval_macro_f1

QuantileTransformer HistGradientBoosting 0.627838 0.598177 0.599152 0.561861
Raw HistGradientBoosting 0.62859 0.598935 0.59866 0.560088
StandardScaler HistGradientBoosting 0.627068 0.596979 0.598817 0.559609

KBinsDiscretizer ExtraTrees 0.999999 0.999999 0.577513 0.535898
Normalizer ExtraTrees 1.0 1.0 0.582915 0.532122
QuantileTransformer ExtraTrees 1.0 1.0 0.584941 0.530738

As we can see, HistGradientBoosting is the most robust model because it avoids the so-called overfitting problem compared to the other models. Moreover, applying continuous transformations, such as Normalizer and Raw, improves the evaluation F1-score and achieves higher performance than the discrete transformation method, KBinsDiscretizer. Thus, continuous transformation methods are more promising than discrete transformation methods. Therefore, we choose HistGradientBoosting as the model for the following experiments.

Feature Scaling-2 (continuous scaling)

Since continuous scaling methods appear to be powerful, we were interested in whether this result could achieve a higher F1-score if we used other continuous scaling methods. Therefore, we reviewed the paper The Impact of Feature Scaling in Machine Learning: Effects on Regression and Classification Tasks and included ten additional scaling methods. Their formulas and results are shown below.

Type Method Formula
1 Min-Max Normalization $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X - X_{\min}}{X_{\max} - X_{\min}}$
2 Max Normalization $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X}{\max(\lvert X \rvert)}$
3 Z-score Normalization $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$
4 Variable Stability Scaling $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\cdot\frac{\mu}{\sigma}$
5 Pareto Scaling $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma}}$
6 Mean Centered $X_{\text{norm}} = X - \mu$
7 Robust Scaler $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X - X_{\text{median}}}{\mathrm{IQR}}$
8 Quantile Transformation $X_{\text{norm}} = F_{\text{target}}^{-1}!\bigl(F_{\text{emp}}(X)\bigr)$
9 Decimal Scaling Normalization $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{X}{10^j}$
10 Tanh Transformation $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\tanh!\left(0.01\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)+1\right]$
11 Logistic Sigmoid Transformation $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-q}},q = \frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$
12 Hyperbolic Tangent Transformation $X_{\text{norm}} = \frac{1-e^{-q}}{1+e^{-q}},q = \frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$

For detailed definitions of the symbols used in these formulas, please refer to the paper.

scaler train_accuracy train_macro_f1 eval_accuracy eval_macro_f1
Logistic Sigmoid Transformation 0.628126 0.598267 0.59912 0.562195
Quantile Transformation 0.627838 0.598177 0.599152 0.561861
Tanh Transformation 0.62706 0.59702 0.598744 0.561458
Max Normalization 0.62859 0.598935 0.598661 0.560089
No 0.62859 0.598935 0.59866 0.560088
Robust Scaler 0.62859 0.598935 0.59866 0.560088
Decimal Scaling Normalization 0.628447 0.598773 0.598491 0.55969
Pareto Scaling 0.627069 0.596979 0.598887 0.559622
Z-score Normalization 0.627068 0.596979 0.598817 0.559609
Mean Centered 0.627068 0.596979 0.598817 0.559609
Min-Max Normalization 0.623864 0.592967 0.598057 0.559577
Hyperbolic Tangent Transformation 0.627061 0.596978 0.598664 0.559445
Variable Stability Scaling 0.628363 0.598586 0.598661 0.558417

As we can see, with the HistGradientBoosting model, the Logistic Sigmoid transformation is the most robust scaling method among the 11 methods presented in the paper. Hence, we choose the Logistic Sigmoid transformation as our scaler.

Parameter Fine Tuning

Since direct grid search for hyperparameter fine-tuning may waste time exploring less important parameter combinations, we adopt the random search method proposed in the paper Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization for hyperparameter tuning. In this paper, the authors propose the following procedures for hyperparameter tuning.

1. Define a hyperparameter search space.
2. Decide the number of trials S based on the computation budget.
3. Randomly sample S hyperparameter configurations.
4. Train one model for each configuration.
5. Evaluate each model on the validation set.
6. Select the configuration with the best validation score.
7. Refit the final model using the selected configuration.

In our case, the specific procedures are as follows:

1. Fix the preprocessing method as LogisticSigmoid.
2. Fix the model as HistGradientBoosting.
3. Randomly sample the hyperparameters of HistGradientBoosting.
4. Select the best hyperparameters based on macro F1 on the internal validation set.
5. Retrain the model on the full training dataset.
6. Finally, evaluate the model on the evaluation dataset.

Since small changes have little impact on learning_rate, max_iter, max_leaf_nodes, and min_samples_leaf when training our models, we sample them using log-uniform or geometric integer distributions. Moreover, since we do not know whether regularization is useful in our experiment, we set l2_regularization to 0 with 50% probability and sample it from a log-uniform distribution with 50% probability. In short, we use the following distribution for each parameter.

Hyperparameter Distributions
learning_rate log-uniform
max_iter geometric integer
max_leaf_nodes geometric integer
min_samples_leaf geometric integer
l2_regularization 50% = 0，50% log-uniform

The best model, with the highest F1-score on the training dataset, has the following hyperparameters, along with its evaluation accuracy and evaluation F1-score.

Parameter Value
learning_rate 0.040865203745585200
max_iter 224
max_leaf_nodes 120
min_samples_leaf 45
l2_regularization 0.0
train_accuracy 0.662802
train_macro_f1 0.637082
eval_accuracy 0.600438
eval_macro_f1 0.560415

From the tables, we observe that although evaluation accuracy shows a slight improvement, the F1-score decreases. This suggests that hyperparameter fine-tuning has limited impact in our problem setting.

Conclusion

In conclusion, we summarize the following interesting findings:

  1. The dataset is unbalanced.
  2. Ensemble methods are more powerful than linear models.
  3. Continuous transformation methods are more promising than discrete transformation methods.
  4. The Logistic Sigmoid transformation is the most robust scaling method.
  5. Hyperparameter fine-tuning has limited impact.

Overall, these results show that by using ensemble models, applying LogisticSigmoid feature scaling, and using random search for hyperparameter tuning, we improved accuracy by about +9.86% (≈ +19.6% relative) and macro F1 by about +16.38% (≈ +41.3% relative) on the evaluation dataset.

Intro

This post provides a step-by-step solution to the online assignment provided by VICI Holdings.

In this project, we use the R-squared value instead of the Mean Squared Error for comparison because it provides a more interpretable measure of performance change.

Moreover, in this setting, minimizing the Mean Squared Error is equivalent to maximizing the R-squared value, since $R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2},$ where $y_i$ denotes the true value, $\hat{y}_i$ denotes the predicted value, $\bar{y}$ denotes the mean of the true values.

TL;DR: By modifying the basic linear regression model, applying feature scaling, and using ensemble methods, we improved the R-squared score on the validation set by 67%.

R-squared Optimization

In the first stage, we build a basic linear regression model using the scikit-learn library, without any regularization terms, special data transformations, or complex models, to serve as our baseline. We then compare the 12 linear models listed on the sklearn.linear_model page and select the top five as our candidate models.

Although we evaluated the 12 continuous scaling methods listed above, the best validation R-squared was still significantly lower than that achieved by kbins_uniform. This result suggests that discretization-based scaling methods are more promising than continuous scaling methods for this task. However, due to time constraints, we only adopt kbins_uniform in the following experiments. In future work, other discretization-based scaling methods could also be explored to further improve R-squared.

Ensemble Methods

Finally, we divide the training dataset into four folds to train the same model on different training sets. We then combine these four models using ensemble methods such as StackingLinear, Weighted Average, Simple Average, and Bagging, and compare their performance with that of non-ensemble methods. We find that models using the StackingLinear ensemble method are the most promising, as this method performed best in our validation results. The result is shown below.

Conclusion

In conclusion, we summarize the following interesting findings:

  1. Basic linear regression models are more promising than more complex models.
  2. Discretization-based scaling methods are more promising than continuous scaling methods.
  3. Models using the StackingLinear ensemble method are the most promising.

Overall, these results show that modifying the basic linear regression model, applying feature scaling, and using ensemble methods can lead to a 67% increase in validation R-squared.
